content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper proposes a method for learning world models that can generalize across different (unseen) dynamics by learning prototypical representations on top of model states and learning a policy with these prototypes as auxiliary inputs to capture context of environments. To encourage contexts at different time steps to be consistent (based on the assumption that dynamics would not change during the trial), time consistent loss is introduced. The method is evaluated on a set of DMC tasks with changing dynamics.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths
- Simple and intuitive method to learn prototypical representations corresponding to contexts and enforce time consistency
- The draft reads well

Weaknesses
- Performance on individual task is not significantly better than baselines; confidence interval largely overlaps in all the tasks. It's shown that the overall performance might be significant but this is likely due to the performance difference in one or two tasks.
- New tasks with changing dynamics are introduced but the draft is missing analysis to show how the performance of all the method changes with changing parameters and how each method is robust to changes in dynamics. For now, it's not clear whether the method really generalizes well or just achieves stronger performance due to better representation learning. For this, I'd like to refer to [1] that shows nice visualization for this.
- It has recently been shown that RSSM could generalize to different visuals or dynamics without introducing additional components (see [2]). Further discussion on the difference to this work could be nice.
- While it has been shown that the model can predict better future states in Figure 6, it's not clear why the method works. More analysis to show that how learned prototypes correspond to different dynamics or contexts is required to further support that the method works as intended.

[1] Ball, Philip J., Cong Lu, Jack Parker-Holder, and Stephen Roberts. "Augmented world models facilitate zero-shot dynamics generalization from a single offline environment." In International Conference on Machine Learning, pp. 619-629. PMLR, 2021.

[2] Lu, Cong, Philip J. Ball, Tim GJ Rudner, Jack Parker-Holder, Michael A. Osborne, and Yee Whye Teh. "Challenges and Opportunities in Offline Reinforcement Learning from Visual Observations." arXiv preprint arXiv:2206.04779 (2022).
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity & Quality
- From the introduction, it's not clear why learning world models with recurrent neural networks is not sufficient for generalization in high-dimensional envs.
- It's a bit difficult to grasp what the proposed time-consistency loss does in a high-level from reading the introduction. More intuitive explanation without details or introducing an additional figure could be helpful
- From reading the draft, it's not clear what exactly 'Dreamer + Context' means.

Originality
- It's not clear introducing the benchmark with changing parameters can be a contribution as DMC with changing dynamics is already introduced in [2, 3].
- Summary of difference to DreamerPro could further strengthen the originality of the proposed approach.

[2] Lu, Cong, Philip J. Ball, Tim GJ Rudner, Jack Parker-Holder, Michael A. Osborne, and Yee Whye Teh. "Challenges and Opportunities in Offline Reinforcement Learning from Visual Observations." arXiv preprint arXiv:2206.04779 (2022).

[3] Dulac-Arnold, Gabriel, Nir Levine, Daniel J. Mankowitz, Jerry Li, Cosmin Paduraru, Sven Gowal, and Todd Hester. "An empirical investigation of the challenges of real-world reinforcement learning." arXiv preprint arXiv:2003.11881 (2020).

content.title: Response to Reviewer NW8q
content.comment:
We sincerely thank you for your efforts in reviewing our paper and your constructive suggestions. We would like to address your concerns as follows.

**Q1. About overall performance.**

A1. Our approach ProtoCAD does not improve performance on only one or two tasks. According to the results in Table 1, on most tasks (6/8), our method achieves the best results over several baselines. Comparable performance is also obtained on the two tasks that are not the best results. Compared to our key baseline Dreamer (which is a strong baseline according to our state-input experiments), ProtoCAD consistently improves the performance on all experimental tasks and delivers 13.2% and 26.7% better mean and median performance across all dynamics generalization tasks.


**Q2. About performance on specific parameter settings.**

A2. Similar to the literature [1], we test different dynamics environments constructed for specific parameter settings separately in the CheetahRun task. Note that the red box shows the parameter settings during training. From the results, we can see that our method has a better generalization ability to different parameter settings.


**Q3. Analysis of the learned features.**

A3. The results from TSNE show that the learned context representation has some differentiated characterization results for different parameter settings. Also, the representation can be generalized to new parameter settings when testing under unseen environments. The learned representation is used as part of the input to the policy network and the value network so that the policy has some generalization ability in new environments as well. 

[1] Philip J Ball, Cong Lu, Jack Parker-Holder, and Stephen Roberts. Augmented world models facilitate zero-shot dynamics generalization from a single offline environment. In International Conference on Machine Learning, pp. 619–629. PMLR, 2021.

content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:

1.The experimental setting is novel and applicable.

2.The paper is written well.

3.The proposed method is straightforward.

Weaknesses:

1.The method proposed is not novel. SwAV is widely utilised in numerous RL and computer vision domains. The further proposed Temporal Consistency appears to  be a incremental trick, and it brings only marginal improvements in relation to Figure 5.

2.The overall method is only able to achieve marginal improvements over the simple baseline: Dreamer+Context (see Figure 3). . The results indicate that the proposed method is incremental.

3.Despite the fact that CaDM, TMCL, and RIA were not initially proposed for high-dimensional control tasks, they can be utilised for such tasks. However, this paper lacks these three essential dynamics generalisation baselines, so the baselines used in this method are weak, and the results do not convincingly demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method.

4.How would the experimental outcomes change if we used multiple time parts instead of two time parts to improve Temporal Consistency?

content.title: Response to Reviewer Z26D
content.comment:
We sincerely thank you for your efforts in reviewing our paper and your constructive suggestions. We would like to address your concerns as follows.

**Q1. About novelty.**

A1. SwAV does have many applications in RL and CV fields. Most of the existing methods use SwAV to extract features from the image input. In this paper, our approach is not simply combining SwAV with RL, but subtly exploiting the unique use of prototypes for the characteristics of SwAV and dynamics generalization problems: using them to extract environmental context features. In addition, the comparison of Dreamer+context with Dreamer also shows that temporal consistency loss is useful for the extraction of context features. 

**Q2. About baselines.**

A2. The original CaDM, TMCL, and RIA utilize planning to obtain actions and assume a known reward function on state transitions during the planning process, which makes them difficult to apply directly to image input tasks. We replace RSSM in Dreamer with CaDM, implementing a version of CaDM for image input, and the results do not work well enough to learn valid policies. However, we can compare our approach to these methods in the state-based MuJoCo environments with the following results (where the results for CaDM, TMCL, and RIA are obtained directly in the RIA paper). 
|           |     CaDM           | TMCL              | RIA       | Dreamer             | ProtoCAD (ours)
|---------|:-----------------:|:-------------------:|-------------------:|:-------------------:|:-------------------:|
|Pendulum     | $-713.95_{\pm21.1}$  | $-691.2_{\pm93.4}$          | $-587.5_{\pm64.4}$ | $-575.9_{\pm56.6}$ | $\boldsymbol{-525.9}_{\pm61.6}$ 
|Ant      | $1660_{\pm57.8}$ | $2994.9_{\pm243.8}$ | $3297.9_{\pm159.7}$  | $4636.3_{\pm412.8}$ |$\boldsymbol{5309.4}_{\pm537.7}$
|Hopper       | $845.2_{\pm20.41}$  | $999.35_{\pm22.8}$          | $1057.4_{\pm37.2}$ | $2107.3_{\pm36.1}$ |$\boldsymbol{2197.8}_{\pm83.44}$
|HalfCheetah     | $5876.6_{\pm799.0}$  | $9039.6_{\pm1065}$ | $\boldsymbol{10859.2}_{\pm465.1}$ | $4701.0_{\pm796.2}$ | $5409.8_{\pm594.1}$
|C\_HalfCheetah | $3656.4_{\pm856.2}$  | $3998.8_{\pm856.2}$           | $\boldsymbol{4819.3}_{\pm409.3}$  | $4593.0_{\pm654.2}$ | $4125.4_{\pm957.9}$ 
|Slim\_Humanoid    | $859.1_{\pm24.01}$  | $2098.7_{\pm109.1}$          | $2432.6_{\pm465.1}$ | $14735_{\pm5842.9}$ |$\boldsymbol{16731.6}_{\pm9595.8}$ 

For state inputs, we use random amplitude scaling [1] for augmentation. The results show that our method substantially outperforms the SOTA method RIA in 4/6 environments. It is worth noting that Dreamer also performs well, showing the ability of RSSM itself to handle in dynamics generalization problems. This also shows that Dreamer is a strong baseline. 

[1] Misha Laskin, Kimin Lee, Adam Stooke, Lerrel Pinto, Pieter Abbeel, and Aravind Srinivas. Reinforcement learning with augmented data. Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems, 33, 2020.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper presents an approach for generalizing to different test-time dynamics than seen during training time through temporally consistent prototypes for context encoding: Prototypical Context-Aware Dynamics (ProtoCAD). ProtoCAD exhibits consistently robust performance on unseen dynamics as compared to a number of baselines across a variety of simulated environments.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
* The general problem of generalization to unseen dynamics is interesting to the research community.
* The problem is well-motivated and the literature review does a good job of contextualizing the paper in prior work.
* The figures are informative and effectively illustrate the benefits of the proposed approach.
* The experiments consider a good number of baselines and many simulation settings, as well as include a thorough ablation study, demonstrating robust performance of ProtoCAD as compared to other methods and support for ProtoCAD's design choices.
* The quantitative and qualitative experiments were fairly thorough with standard errors across multiple random seeds.
    
Weaknesses:
* The quality of the writing could be improved. There were many repetitive, not very clear phrases (e.g., "the introduce SwAV into RL to help only represent learning") and several long, convoluted sentences (e.g., "ProtoCAD extracts ..." in the abstract). I am also unclear on what 'a finite number of dynamics' means.
* I did not find where in the paper the two data augmentation techniques were specified. Is it explained in Sec. 4.1, 'we perform bilinear interpolation of the random shifts and ensure consistency of the augmentation across time steps'? So, the inputs are randomly shifted and then interpolated? It should also be explained why two channels are necessary. My understanding is that one channel focuses on learning the encoding, while the other handles prototype learning. Is that correct?
* There is abuse of notation: $M$ refers to both a POMDP model and a temporal index to divide the sequence into two parts.
* Some statements are not very precise in their current form. For example, 'a fundamental characteristic of context is that it does not change within a trajectory'. Although I understand that the authors are referring to concepts like mass, context needs to be defined better here. For example, in deformable objects, their shape may change, etc.
* If I am understanding correctly, one of the key components of novelty in this paper is adding temporal consistency into the SwAV loss. The differences with the original SwAV loss should be better highlighted and the intuition for how temporal consistency is enforced in the current formulation (Eq. 5) should be included, particularly since this is a key aspect of the contribution.  
* One of the baselines, Dreamer+Context, seems to use the temporally consistent SwAV loss to condition RL on context. I was not clear on the difference between this baseline and the ProtoCAD method. Is it that Dreamer+Context does not use prototypes?
* The highlighted summary quantitative performance in the text and the qualitative example focus on a comparison to Dreamer. It would be more compelling to highlight comparisons to one of the stronger baselines, like DreamerPro.
* Quantitative comparison for long-term predictions would be helpful to include across the considered methods.
* In Table 1, are the listed +/- values standard errors or standard deviations?
* It was not clear why the comparison to DreamerV2 was not included in the main experiments, and without justification appears to be a bit of an after-thought.

Some typos and points of confusion are listed below:
1. Throughout the paper, I believe 'temporal consistent prototypes' should read 'temporally consistent prototypes'.
2. Abstract: 'comparing the feature' -> 'comparing the features'.
3. Sec. 1, third paragraph: looks like there may be some extra spaces in a few places.
4. Sec. 2, third paragraph: the acronym MBRL (model-based reinforcement learning) was not defined previously.
5. Sec. 3.1, second paragraph: 'different $c \in \mathcal{C}$ leads to different POMDP' -> 'different $c \in \mathcal{C}$ lead to different POMDP models'.
6. Sec. 3.1, second paragraph: 'mass of a pendulum can be a context' -> 'mass of a pendulum can be considered contextual information'.
7. Sec. 4.2, second paragraph: 'that projects maps to' -> 'that projections map to'.
8. Sec. 5.1, baselines: 'start-of-the-art' -> 'state-of-the-art'. The SOTA acronym should also be introduced here as it is used later on.
9. Sec. 5.1, baselines: 'argumentation' -> 'augmentation'.
10. The references should be proofread (e.g., to ensure the conference name formatting is consistent in terms of capitalization, etc.).
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The novelty in the paper appears to be in the method for learning and using the prototypes and modifying the existing SwAV loss to be temporally consistent. It would be helpful to better highlight these points of novelty as compared to existing work. The clarity could also be improved in terms of the purpose for the two different architecture branches and the workings of the temporal consistency component of the loss. The code was not included with the paper, which hurts reproducibility.
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall, the paper presents a method for conditioning RL on dynamics context and improving generalization to unseen dynamics settings. The authors do their due diligence in considering several baselines across many simulation settings, demonstrating robust performance of the proposed ProtoCAD method. However, the presentation of the current version of the paper could be improved to better highlight the specific advancements over prior work and provide the intuition for the design choices in the approach.

content.title: Response to Reviewer degt
content.comment:
We sincerely thank you for your efforts in reviewing our paper and your constructive suggestions. We would like to address your concerns as follows.

**Q1. Why two channels of data augmentation?**

A1. The two views augmentation is obtained by applying random shifts with bilinear interpolation. We ensure that the augmentation is consistent across time steps. We assume that the samples of both channels have the same dynamics after the augmentation. The whole framework is to make the samples under both views belong to the same class as much as possible. For this purpose, we compute an assignment probability $w$ and assign the samples in batch to the $K$ classes according to $w$ so that the samples that are similar to the prototype (large inner product) are grouped together.

**Q2. Regarding quantitative comparisons, it would be more compelling to highlight comparisons to one of the stronger baselines, like DreamerPro.**

A2. The motivation for DreamerPro is that it does not require reconstruction. In the original paper, we did not make changes to the model of DreamerPro and thus could not obtain visualization results of its multi-step reconstructed images. In a subsequent revision, we will add a reconstruction module to DreamerPro to examine its multi-step prediction capability.


**Q3. It was not clear why the comparison to DreamerV2 was not included in the main experiments, and without justification appears to be a bit of an after-thought.**

A3. The experimental comparison with DreamerV2 is in standard DMC environments and does not involve dynamics variation, which is different from the main experiment. Therefore, the results of this experiment are placed in the appendix. The comparison with DreamerV2 has two main reasons: first, to verify that our method can still work in the standard DMC environments, and second, to verify that our method can be incorporated with different versions of the world model.


**Q4. The code was not included with the paper, which hurts reproducibility.**

A4. We will open the source code after the publication of this work.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper investigates the dynamics generalization problem in model-based reinforcement learning. Built on the RSSM model, this paper uses data augmentation and self-supervised learning to learn hidden states and uses the Sinkhorn-Knopp algorithm to cluster the states into prototypes. Finally, a consistency loss is added to ensure that one trajectory is in only one environment.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength

1. The proposed method is simple and intuitive. The empirical studies show that the proposed method has some advantages over baseline methods.

2. The paper is well structured and presented. The method is explained clearly. 

Weakness

Overall, the proposed method is a combination of existing ideas to address a specific problem of dynamics generalization. While the combination of existing ideas is not necessarily a disadvantage, the motivation for the combination and choice of specific methods is not clear. In the rebuttal, I would like to see how the authors address the following specific concerns.

Why can the proposed method be generalizable to a new environment? Enforcing the similarity of representation on a single trajectory seems heuristic. Having some theory that formalizes the dynamics generalization problem and proves the generalization ability under certain conditions would be more helpful to explain the motivation and principle behind the proposed method.  If the theoretical analysis might be difficult to establish, some simulations with known ground-truth would be useful to demonstrate some properties of the proposed method.

Is temporal consistency a sufficient condition for dynamics generalization?

Why is the Sinkhorn-Knopp method used here? The reason that this algorithm was used for assisting RL is not convincing, as they are addressing different aspects of RL. A comparison with at least a more recent method is needed.

In section 3.2, “we denote the deterministic output by f”, where is the f in the equations? Similarly, the paragraph above Eq 3 also has this definition f, but I couldn’t see where it is used.

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Paper3950 by Reviewer U5c9

content.title: Response to Reviewer U5c9
content.comment:
We sincerely thank you for your efforts in reviewing our paper and your constructive suggestions. We would like to address your concerns as follows.

**Q1. Why can the proposed method be generalizable to a new environment?**

A1. Our motivation is to extract the environment context information from the state trajectories produced by RSSM to assist in policy learning. Sinkhorn-Knopp can cluster trajectory data of batch and use prototypes to fit the different situations encountered in the learning process. The learned prototypes can characterize the context information. The results from TSNE show that the learned context representation has some differentiated characterization results for different parameter settings. Also, the representation can be generalized to new parameter settings when testing under unseen environments. The learned representation is used as part of the input to the policy network and the value network so that the policy has some generalization ability in new environments as well. 

**Q2. Is temporal consistency a sufficient condition for dynamics generalization?**

A2. In our setting, dynamics does not change in the middle of an episode, so we expect that the extracted context representation information is consistent across a trajectory. Therefore, a context representation that is valid for dynamics generalization should be temporally consistent, but a representation that only guarantees temporal consistency is not necessarily valid for dynamics generalization. Thus, in our framework, prototypes are learned simultaneously to summarize the state trajectory characteristics. 


**Q3. Why is the Sinkhorn-Knopp method used here?**

A3. Sinkhorn-Knopp is a common practice in SwAV-like approaches [1, 2, 3, 4]. According to the literature, in practice, good performance can be obtained using only a small number of iterations with the Sinkhorn-Knopp algorithm. Since ProtoCAD is an online operation, Sinkhorn-Knopp is better suited for our task. Moreover, we keep the same clustering algorithm for a fair comparison. 

[1] Mathilde Caron, Ishan Misra, Julien Mairal, Priya Goyal, Piotr Bojanowski, and Armand Joulin. Unsupervised learning of visual features by contrasting cluster assignments. Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems, 33:9912–9924, 2020. 

[2] Denis Yarats, Rob Fergus, Alessandro Lazaric, and Lerrel Pinto. Reinforcement learning with prototypical representations. In International Conference on Machine Learning, pp. 11920–11931. PMLR, 2021a.

[3] Bogdan Mazoure, Ahmed M Ahmed, R Devon Hjelm, Andrey Kolobov, and Patrick MacAlpine. Cross-trajectory representation learning for zero-shot generalization in RL. In International Conference on Learning Representations, 2022.

[4] Fei Deng, Ingook Jang, and Sungjin Ahn. DreamerPro: Reconstruction-free model-based reinforcement learning with prototypical representations. In International Conference on Machine Learning, pp. 4956–4975. PMLR, 2022.
